titre: Sudbury, 1.85 Billion Years Ago: An Impact May Have Ended Banded Iron
accroche: 1.85 billion years ago, banded iron deposition stops near Lake Superior. The USGS sees the mark of a giant impact.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the Lake Superior region, rocks striped with red and gray bands tell, layer by layer, an episode in the history of the ocean: banded iron formations. The oldest known, in Greenland, have an estimated age of 3.7 to 3.8 billion years; the most massive, in Western Australia (Hamersley), were deposited between 2,470 and 2,450 million years ago, over more than 900 meters of thickness.

## An Iron That Water Dissolved, Then No Longer Did

Before the atmosphere held oxygen in lasting amounts, the deep oceans were rich in dissolved ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), supplied by the weathering of continents and by hydrothermal vents. Once this iron met water where photosynthetic organisms had produced oxygen, it oxidized into insoluble ferric iron (Fe³⁺) and settled to the bottom in layers alternating with silica. This is the model associated with geologist Preston Cloud, whose 1968 paper deals with the early atmosphere and oceans of the Earth: the oxygen produced reacted with the iron dissolved in the water and formed the deposits.

## A Halt the USGS Links to an Impact

In the Lake Superior region, the end of deposition of most of these formations falls around 1.85 billion years ago, after a period of about 1.1 billion years of episodic deposits. The explanation that comes to mind first is a gradual oxygenation of the deep waters. But in 2009, two researchers, John Slack and William Cannon, proposed in the journal Geology another cause for this halt: it coincides with the oceanic impact of the giant Sudbury bolide, in present-day Ontario, also dated to 1.85 billion years ago. According to them, this impact would have globally mixed the surface waters with the anoxic deep waters, creating a suboxic state of the ocean. That state would have prevented hydrothermal iron from being carried from the deep ocean to the continental margins, where banded iron formed.

## What This Changes

The usual story of Earth's oxygenation is a slope: life produces oxygen, and the atmosphere and ocean gradually take it up. Slack and Cannon's hypothesis introduces an extraterrestrial event into it: the Sudbury crater, with an original diameter of about 130 kilometers, is one of the largest known on Earth, after Vredefort and Chicxulub. Its age of 1.849 billion years is established by uranium-lead dating of zircons (Donald Davis, 2008). It is a hypothesis, then, not an established fact: banded iron does not only tell the rise of oxygen, it may also keep the trace of the day an impact upended an ocean.

carte.punch: A giant impact may have stopped 1.1 billion years of banded iron.
carte.idee: Banded iron deposition stops in the Lake Superior region around 1.85 billion years ago. A 2009 USGS study links this halt to the impact of the giant Sudbury bolide, dated to the same period, which may have mixed the ocean's waters.

quiz.question: According to the Slack and Cannon study (2009), what does the end of banded iron deposition in the Lake Superior region, around 1.85 billion years ago, coincide with?
choix: The appearance of the first animals in the oceans
The impact of the giant Sudbury bolide, dated to the same period
A glaciation that would have frozen all the world's oceans
The complete disappearance of oxygen from the atmosphere
quiz.explication: Slack and Cannon, USGS researchers, link the end of deposition to the impact of the Sudbury bolide, dated to 1.85 billion years ago, which may have mixed the ocean's waters. The other options do not appear in their study.
